forces.title: Global payments revenue growth moderating significantly
forces.description: Global payments revenue growth is projected to slow from an average annual rate of 9% (2020–2025) to 4% (2025–2030). This moderation signals a structural transition in the global payments landscape, where growth will depend more on competitive advantages like operational discipline and technological leadership rather than broad market momentum. This reduction in growth velocity impacts all regions, including EMEA and the UK.
forces.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

forces.title: Payments revenues shifting from NII to fee-based structures
forces.description: As interest rate tailwinds soften globally, the revenue mix in payments is expected to shift from 46% net interest income (NII) and 54% fee income in 2025 to 44% NII and 56% fee income by 2030. This structural shift, particularly pronounced in EMEA due to lower interest rates and margin compression, requires financial institutions to adapt their monetization strategies, placing greater emphasis on fee resilience and yield discipline.
forces.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

forces.title: Agentic AI threatens payments and deposit profit pools
forces.description: Agentic artificial intelligence is poised to disrupt payments economics by enabling autonomous software agents to optimize account yields and dynamically route transactions to minimize fees or maximize rewards. This could put $75-160 billion in global payments revenue at risk by 2030, primarily from declining deposit net interest income and consumer credit card revenues. This poses a significant challenge to traditional revenue streams for UK banks and payments providers.
forces.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

forces.title: Stablecoins and tokenized deposits bypass traditional revenue streams
forces.description: Digital assets like stablecoins and tokenized deposits pose an additional headwind to payments and deposit revenues. They bypass traditional interchange and foreign-exchange (FX) conversion markups, and shift float income out of commercial bank deposits. As cross-border corporate corridors increasingly adopt tokenized settlement, providers will face direct margin pressure on foreign-exchange spreads and correspondent banking fees, affecting global and UK institutions.
forces.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

forces.title: Payment infrastructure fragmenting into regional, multi-rail competitive arenas
forces.description: Rather than converging, global payment infrastructure is fragmenting into regional, multi-rail competitive arenas. Institutions in card-resilient markets like the UK need to navigate competing pressures from zero-fee domestic real-time account-to-account (A2A) networks, legacy card perimeters, and wholesale stablecoin corridors. This fragmentation complicates global payments strategy and requires navigating diverse regulatory and economic conditions.
forces.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

forces.title: Non-bank players increasing competition in financing and trading
forces.description: Non-bank financial institutions are becoming more prominent, with about 40% of corporates open to using non-bank financing (fintechs, private credit, direct institutional lending) over the next three years. Non-bank market makers (NBMMs) already capture 9-14% of wallet share by asset class in trading. These challengers offer advantages like structured flexibility, speed, digital experience, and technological sophistication, creating wallet leakage risks for incumbent banks in the UK and globally.
forces.source_title: Anchor or drift: What it takes to capture wallet share in 2026

forces.title: Customer primacy shifting towards digital-native challengers
forces.description: Neobanks and fintechs now hold over a quarter (27%) of all UK banking relationships, a significant increase from low single digits a decade ago. These digital-native competitors are increasingly capturing transactions and daily engagement, unbundling the traditional relationship between primary accounts and customers' financial lives. This shift in primacy threatens incumbents' stable, inexpensive deposit bases and their ability to cross-sell.
forces.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

forces.title: Commercial banking value shifts from balance sheet to transaction layer
forces.description: Competition in UK commercial banking is intensifying as value increasingly shifts from traditional balance sheet lending to the transaction layer (e.g., cash management, payments, FX). Over 60% of UK commercial-banking revenue already sits outside lending. Incumbents risk retaining credit relationships while other providers capture transactions, data, and engagement, which are crucial for future revenue growth and cross-selling opportunities.
forces.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

forces.title: AI-driven disintermediation threatens bank deposit profits
forces.description: AI significantly lowers the friction in comparing rates, switching accounts, and moving money, historically protecting incumbent banks' deposit bases. Agentic AI assistants can automatically sweep idle cash to higher-yield accounts, potentially reducing deposit profits by 20% or more if just 5-10% of balances migrate. This rapid disintermediation threatens a core source of cheap and sticky funding for UK banks.
forces.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

forces.title: AI reshapes insurance operating models and economics across all lines
forces.description: AI is fundamentally transforming the insurance operating model, extending beyond individual business lines. It creates new liability exposures for AI-embedded products and systems, impacts distribution through agentic commerce, and structurally shifts industry economics by automating back/middle-office activities, thereby lowering expense ratios. Furthermore, AI improves risk assessment and prevention through continuous monitoring and proactive engagement with policyholders, leading to a profound change in the insurance value chain globally, including the UK.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: New high-growth industries create complex, systemic insurance risks
forces.description: Eighteen high-growth industries ("arenas") are introducing novel, complex, and systemic risk exposures that existing insurance products were not designed to cover. These arenas lead to less frequent but significantly more severe claims, requiring new coverage categories, liability frameworks, and risk-sharing structures. Examples include EV battery fires, autonomous vehicle liabilities, and cyber catastrophe bonds. This represents a fundamental shift for life and P&C insurers in the UK, creating both challenges and opportunities for product innovation.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Insurance industry faces moderate growth phase post-rate-driven expansion
forces.description: The insurance industry, particularly P&C, is entering a more moderate growth phase after a period where premium expansion was primarily driven by rate increases rather than underlying coverage expansion. As rate growth has slowed, overall premium growth has decelerated, with limited expansion in underlying coverage in many markets. This necessitates insurers globally, including in the UK, to seek profitable growth beyond traditional lines and mature risk pools, impacting their top-line potential.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Obesity drugs to rewrite mortality and morbidity assumptions
forces.description: GLP-1 receptor drugs have the potential to significantly change the disease burden, which forms the basis for life, disability, and annuities pricing. Trial data show a 20% reduction in major cardiovascular events, and Munich Re estimates 0.2-0.5% annual mortality improvement for 20 years. This requires life and annuity providers in the UK to reassess pricing, reserving, and longevity assumptions, as existing policies priced on pre-GLP-1 assumptions may systematically overprice treated populations.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Genetic data enabling individualized life insurance risk assessment
forces.description: Advances in genomics and personalized medicine are shifting life insurance from pooled risk models to highly individualized mortality and morbidity assessments. As genetic data becomes more predictive, the actuarial basis of life pricing moves towards individual-level risk profiles, fundamentally altering how life risk is segmented. This trend will require UK life insurers to integrate genomic insights into underwriting, navigate disclosure rules, and adapt to ethical and regulatory questions surrounding genetic information use.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Electric vehicle adoption drives higher auto claims severity
forces.description: The increasing adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is propelling higher claims severity in auto insurance. Battery damage frequently leads to total-loss write-offs, and repairs can cost 20-30% more than for internal combustion engine equivalents. Additionally, thermal runaway introduces a fire propagation risk that crosses from auto into property lines, particularly for home garages. This compounds exposure for UK insurers, with fewer claims but significantly higher per-claim costs.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Autonomous vehicles shift auto risk to systemic, commercial liabilities
forces.description: As shared autonomous vehicles (SAVs) deploy, risk is migrating from frequent, human-error-driven claims to less frequent but higher-severity, correlated system risks such as software defects, outages, and cyberattacks across fleets. Liability shifts from individual drivers to platforms, OEMs, and technology providers, fundamentally reshaping personal auto policies. McKinsey research suggests billions in personal auto premiums will migrate to commercial insurance, representing a major structural change for UK auto insurers.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: AI-enabled cyber threats pose systemic correlation risk for commercial P&C
forces.description: Cyber risk has evolved to dynamic threat environments amplified by AI-enabled attacks. The fundamental challenge for commercial P&C insurers is systemic correlation, where a single software vulnerability can trigger simultaneous claims across thousands of policyholders, akin to a natural catastrophe. This means traditional portfolio diversification offers less protection, and tail correlations exceed traditional reinsurance capacity, demanding new capital structures and advanced risk analytics for UK insurers.
forces.source_title: The strategic new arenas reshaping insurance

forces.title: Incumbent banks leverage customer trust for AI service adoption
forces.description: Incumbent banks in the UK possess a significant advantage in customer trust, with 64% of AI users preferring their primary bank for AI services over tech companies or fintechs. This trust provides a critical opening for banks to become the trusted AI interface for customers. By quickly building on this foundation and deploying AI-enabled solutions, banks can turn AI from a disintermediation threat into a powerful tool for customer engagement and retention.
forces.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

forces.title: Annual client banking wallet reallocation creates continuous contest
forces.description: Banking relationships are no longer evergreen, with clients continuously optimizing their provider ecosystems. Surveyed corporates reallocate 12-13% of their wallet share annually, institutional investors 17%, and financial sponsors up to 25%. This continuous reallocation, driven by performance, event-driven shifts, or strategic rebalancing, means banks must re-earn contestable wallet share every year, particularly in high-yield flow and event products.
forces.source_title: Anchor or drift: What it takes to capture wallet share in 2026

forces.title: Client demand for AI-enabled relationship managers to drive engagement
forces.description: Clients decisively prefer engagement centered on relationship managers (RMs), expecting them to be faster, more responsive, and deeply understand client needs. Corporates require RMs to orchestrate rapid, tailored solutions and facilitate seamless execution. This structural shift necessitates banks to reengineer coverage models by segment, equipping RMs with real-time AI tools and institutionalized senior sponsorship to proactively deliver client outcomes and secure valuable wallet share.
forces.source_title: Anchor or drift: What it takes to capture wallet share in 2026

viewpoints.title: EMEA payments face margin compression and slow growth ahead
viewpoints.description: The payments sector in Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), which includes the UK, is expected to experience significantly slower annual growth, moderating to about 3% between 2025 and 2030, down sharply from 14% in 2020-2025. This decline is attributed to lower interest rates, which are compressing treasury and deposit margins. As a result, providers are being prompted to shift rapidly towards fee-based structures. This indicates a challenging environment for payments firms in the region due to structural and cyclical pressures.
viewpoints.source_title: The 2026 Global Payments Report: Operational excellence in an invisible world

viewpoints.title: UK financial services exports anchor in advanced economies, diversify towards Asia
viewpoints.description: The UK's financial services exports are heavily concentrated in advanced economies, with the EU and US collectively accounting for approximately two-thirds of the sector's total exports. However, there's a visible trend of diversification towards faster-growing emerging markets, particularly in Asia (China, Hong Kong, Singapore, GCC, Asia-Pacific Other). This indicates a dual strategy for the UK, maintaining strong traditional ties while gradually expanding into new, dynamic corridors, which could enhance long-term economic resilience.
viewpoints.source_title: Global financial services trade in transition

viewpoints.title: UK stands as world's second-largest financial services exporter
viewpoints.description: The UK is identified as the world's second-largest financial services exporter, showcasing its significant global reach and established international financial centre status. Despite a higher degree of market concentration compared to the US (the largest exporter), the UK maintains a distinctive, internationally-oriented position. This highlights the substantial scale and importance of the UK's financial services sector on a global stage, providing a strong foundation for continued trade and connectivity.
viewpoints.source_title: Global financial services trade in transition

viewpoints.title: UK banks highly profitable but face increasing strategic vulnerability
viewpoints.description: UK banks are currently experiencing their most profitable period in years, with returns on tangible equity (ROTE) in the mid-to-high teens. However, this profitability masks increasing strategic vulnerability due to eroding foundations. Investor skepticism is evident, with the sector trading at a 52% discount to other industries on book value. The grace period for UK banks is closing rapidly, particularly due to the accelerating pace of AI adoption, which creates both opportunities and significant competitive threats.
viewpoints.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

viewpoints.title: Investor skepticism remains high despite UK banking profitability
viewpoints.description: Despite UK banks reporting high profitability, with some achieving ROTE in the twenties, the banking sector in the UK trades at approximately a 52% discount to other industries on book value. This significant discount indicates that investors remain highly skeptical about the durability of these strong economic performances. The underlying concern suggests structural weaknesses or future challenges that could impact sustained profitability, leading to a cautious outlook on the sector's long-term value.
viewpoints.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

viewpoints.title: AI accelerates competitive pressure, closing grace period for UK banks
viewpoints.description: The advent of AI is rapidly compressing the window for UK banks to adapt to competitive shifts. Unlike previous technological changes that allowed incumbents ample time to respond, AI adoption is happening at unprecedented speed among customers. This swift adoption makes it easier for consumers to compare providers, switch products, and move money, fundamentally threatening the traditional banking model and increasing the urgency for banks to overhaul their operations and customer engagement strategies.
viewpoints.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking

viewpoints.title: Incumbent banks hold trust advantage for AI services, but action is critical
viewpoints.description: Among AI users in the UK, 64% would trust their primary bank most to offer AI services, significantly higher than trust in major technology companies (16%) or independent fintechs (8%). This indicates a strong foundation of trust that incumbents can leverage. However, this advantage is perishable, as 49% of consumers would consider a third-party financial AI service if their bank offered none, highlighting the urgency for banks to quickly build on this trust with their own AI solutions.
viewpoints.source_title: The decade to redefine UK banking
